pairs.right: More of the metal's value earned inside the country

pairs.why: Storage cuts waste and steadies income.
pairs.left: Cold stores at a fishing port
pairs.right: Catch sold later at a better price instead of spoiling

pairs.why: Investing resource revenue diversifies the economy.
pairs.left: A state fund built from oil revenue
pairs.right: Money for schools and roads after the wells run dry

recall.prompt: Match each primary-industry project to the development gain it aims for:
distractors: A rise in the price of imported cars

sections.keyIdea: Developing farming, mining, forestry and fishing uses a country's natural advantages and can fund wider development, if the revenue is invested and the resource well managed.
sections.examMatters: Say which constraint this strategy eases (foreign currency) and which it can worsen (volatility, the terms of trade); weighing the two for the country in the question is the evaluation.

realExample.text: Botswana used its diamond revenue to pay for roads, schools and clinics, and grew from one of the poorest countries at independence into an upper-middle-income economy.

sections.misconception: Students set primary industries against development. Many rich economies began with farming or mining; the question is whether the income is invested in diversifying the economy or captured by a few.

body.text: **Aid** is the transfer of resources to a developing country on better terms than the market offers: grants, loans at low interest, food, equipment or expertise. It may come from one government or through institutions such as the World Bank. **Tied aid** must be spent on goods from the donor country.

In Harrod-Domar terms, aid fills the savings and foreign currency gaps. If Karanda invests aid worth 2% of GDP on top of its 12% saving, growth rises from 3% to 14 ÷ 4 = 3.5%. Humanitarian aid saves lives in a disaster; development aid can fund clinics, vaccination and schools directly.

**Debt relief** cancels or reduces a country's overseas debt, freeing the foreign currency and tax revenue that servicing absorbed. If Karanda's debt service fell from 15% to 5% of its $12bn export earnings, $1.2bn a year would be freed. Critics argue aid can create dependency, be captured by corrupt officials or serve the donor's interests, and that relief can reward past overborrowing.

sections.title: Aid and Debt Relief

hints: the savings ratio divided by the capital-output ratio
saving plus aid, divided by the capital-output ratio
the fall in the share, times export earnings
recall.prompt: Work out what aid and debt relief do for a different country:
template: It saves 8% of GDP with a capital-output ratio of 2, so it grows at ___ a year.
Aid worth 2% of GDP, all of it invested, lifts growth to ___ a year.
If debt service falls from 25% to 10% of $10bn of export earnings, $___bn a year is freed.

sections.keyIdea: Aid and debt relief add foreign resources a poor country lacks; whether they promote development depends on what they are spent on and the conditions attached.
sections.examMatters: When a question gives aid as a share of GDP, add it to domestic saving to show the Harrod-Domar effect, then evaluate with where the money goes and who controls it.

realExample.text: Under the Heavily Indebted Poor Countries initiative and the relief that followed it, more than 30 countries, most of them in Africa, had much of their overseas debt cancelled on condition that the savings went on reducing poverty.

sections.misconception: Students treat aid as either always good or always wasted. The evidence depends on the type: humanitarian aid and health programmes such as vaccination have clear effects, while large budget transfers to weak governments have much weaker ones.

body.text: **The World Bank** is an international institution owned by its member governments. It lends for long-term development: roads, power, water, schools, health systems and reforms of how governments work. Its International Development Association gives grants and loans at very low interest to the poorest countries.

**The International Monetary Fund (IMF)** exists to keep the international monetary system stable. It lends to countries that cannot pay for their imports or debts — a balance of payments crisis, the foreign currency gap in its sharpest form — and it monitors and advises its members.

IMF loans usually come with **conditions**: cutting the budget deficit, removing subsidies, raising interest rates, letting the currency fall, privatising. Supporters argue the conditions fix the causes of the crisis and restore confidence, so private lenders and investors return. Critics argue they cut spending on health and education when the poor most need it, deepen recessions and impose one model on very different economies.

sections.title: The World Bank and the IMF

groups.why: Each is long-term finance for development projects.
groups.name: The World Bank
items: A 30-year loan to build a hydroelectric dam
A grant to train rural health workers in the poorest countries
Finance for a new national road network

groups.why: Each is about short-term stability: crisis lending, conditions and surveillance.
groups.name: The IMF
items: An emergency loan to a country that cannot pay for its imports
A condition that the borrower cuts its budget deficit
A yearly check on a member economy's policies

recall.prompt: Sort each activity into the World Bank's role or the IMF's role:

sections.keyIdea: The World Bank lends for long-term development projects; the International Monetary Fund lends short-term to countries in balance of payments crisis, usually with conditions.
sections.examMatters: The specification asks for their role (3d). An Evaluate on the IMF weighs the stability its loans restore against the social cost of its conditions, for the country in the question.

realExample.text: Pakistan and Sri Lanka have both turned to the IMF when they ran short of foreign currency; the loans came with conditions to raise tax revenue and cut energy subsidies.

sections.misconception: Students confuse the two institutions. The World Bank finances long-term development; the IMF lends short-term to countries in a balance of payments crisis. Both are owned by member governments and both lend with conditions.

body.text: **Non-government organisations (NGOs)** are independent of governments and do not seek profit. They include international charities such as Oxfam and Médecins Sans Frontières and local organisations such as BRAC in Bangladesh. They are funded by donations, grants from governments and, sometimes, their own enterprises.

Their role in development: delivering emergency relief; running schools, clinics, clean-water and microfinance projects; training farmers; and campaigning, for example for debt relief. Working at community level, they can reach remote villages and target the poorest, often at lower cost and with less corruption than state programmes.

Their limits: they work on a small scale compared with governments; their funding is uncertain and can follow donors' priorities rather than local needs; many projects stop when the NGO leaves; and running services alongside the state can weaken it. They complement governments and the international institutions rather than replace them.

sections.title: Non-Government Organisations

groups.why: Each reflects reach and targeting at community level.
groups.name: Strength
items: A charity health worker reaches a village with no road
Donations go straight to the families who lost their homes
A local group knows which households are poorest

groups.why: Each reflects small scale, uncertain funding or donor-driven priorities.
groups.name: Limitation
items: The water project stops when the grant runs out after three years
A donor's favourite cause gets funded before what villagers need
The charity runs ten clinics where the country needs a thousand

recall.prompt: Sort each statement into a strength or a limitation of NGOs in development:

sections.keyIdea: NGOs are independent, non-profit organisations that deliver aid and services directly to communities, often reaching people that governments and markets miss.
sections.examMatters: The role of NGOs is its own bullet in 3d. Compare them with the World Bank and the IMF on scale, targeting and accountability — that comparison is the evaluation an essay on institutions needs.

realExample.text: BRAC began as a small relief effort in Bangladesh and now runs schools, health programmes and microfinance serving millions of people across Asia and Africa.

sections.misconception: Students treat NGOs as the solution governments failed to find. Their strength is reach and targeting at small scale; national problems such as infrastructure or macroeconomic stability still need governments and institutions.

takeaway: Lewis: surplus labour moves to industry until the turning point.
Tourism, primary industries, aid and debt relief each help and leak.
World Bank: long-term projects. IMF: crisis loans. NGOs: local reach.

notes.title: Measuring Development

items.text: Economic development — an improvement in living standards and welfare: health, education, income and freedom, not output alone.
Human Development Index (HDI) — a composite index of health (life expectancy at birth), education (mean and expected years of schooling) and income (GNI per head at PPP).
Other measures — adult male labour in agriculture; access to clean water; energy consumption per capita; internet, mobile phones and doctors per thousand of population.
Geometric mean: a weak dimension pulls the index down more than an arithmetic mean would.
Measures of poverty and inequality within a country are topic 4.3.4.

notes.keyIdea: How development differs from growth, how the HDI is built and where it falls short, and the six other measures of development the specification names.
takeaway: Growth helps pay for development; it does not guarantee it.
An average hides who gains; the data are weakest where it matters most.
Use single indicators alongside the HDI, not instead of it.

notes.title: Constraints: Commodities, Savings and Currency

items.text: Prebisch-Singer hypothesis — primary product prices tend to fall relative to manufactures over time, so primary exporters' terms of trade decline.
Harrod-Domar model — growth = savings ratio ÷ capital-output ratio. The savings gap is the saving needed for a target growth rate minus actual saving.
Foreign currency gap — the foreign currency a growth plan needs minus what the country earns. Capital flight — residents moving their money abroad.
Copper 60% of exports × a 25% price fall = export earnings down 15%.
Terms of trade 90 ÷ 120 × 100 = 75. Harrod-Domar 12 ÷ 4 = 3%; 6% needs 24%: a gap of 12 points.
Exports $12bn against import needs of $14bn: a foreign currency gap of $2bn.

notes.keyIdea: Five economic constraints that all come down to too little saving, too little foreign currency, or earnings that swing.
takeaway: Volatility, not only low prices, makes planning impossible.
Harrod-Domar points to foreign savings to fill the gap.
Capital flight drains savings and foreign currency at once.

notes.title: Constraints: People, Debt, Credit and Infrastructure

items.text: Dependency ratio — people under 15 and over 64 per 100 of working age.
Household debt — what families owe; overseas debt — what a country owes abroad, serviced in foreign currency.
Access to credit and banking — whether people can save safely and borrow for productive projects.
Karanda: (42 + 4) ÷ 54 × 100 = 85 dependants per hundred.
Debt service $1.8bn = 15% of export earnings, gone before any import is bought.
No collateral, no loan, no machine: the savings gap seen from below.

notes.keyIdea: Five constraints on the people, the finance and the physical capital an economy needs to grow.
takeaway: Fast population growth eats the rise in output.
Debt constrains when its cost exceeds what it produced.
Missing infrastructure and skills raise every cost.

notes.title: Non-Economic Constraints

items.text: Corruption — abuse of public office for private gain. Poor governance — the state failing to provide reliable rules, courts and policy.
Brain drain — emigration of skilled workers. Remittances — money migrants send home.
Corruption: a hidden tax on investment, and production inside the frontier.
Civil war: capital destroyed and workers lost — the frontier shifts inward.
Migration also appears as a demographic factor in 2a.

notes.keyIdea: Corruption, poor governance, civil wars, migration and terrorism: constraints that are not economic in origin but act through investment and capacity.
takeaway: Name the mechanism, not just the moral point.
War shrinks capacity; corruption wastes it.
Migration both costs and returns resources.

notes.title: Market-Orientated Strategies

items.text: Trade liberalisation — removing barriers to trade. FDI — a foreign firm investing in productive assets it controls.
Privatisation — selling state-owned firms to private owners. Floating exchange rate — a value set by the market.
Microfinance — small loans and savings for people banks will not serve, often through groups.
FDI of 6% plus saving of 12%: growth 3% → 4.5%.
Falling export earnings → depreciation → cheaper exports, with no reserves spent.
How trade barriers work is 4.3.2; exchange rate systems as such are 4.3.3.

notes.keyIdea: Six market-orientated strategies: open trade, attract investment, withdraw subsidies and state ownership, let the currency float, and bring credit to the poor.
takeaway: Each strategy answers a named constraint.
Gains depend on links to local firms and on competition.
The costs fall on identifiable groups.

notes.title: Interventionist Strategies

items.text: Human capital — the skills, knowledge and health that make people productive.
Managed exchange rate — market-set but steered by the central bank. Joint venture — a TNC and a local partner sharing ownership.
Buffer stock scheme — buying at a floor price and selling at a ceiling price to hold the price in a band.
Coffee: bumper harvest of 480k tonnes → $1.60; the agency buys 80k tonnes to hold $2.00.
Poor harvest of 300k tonnes → $2.50; the agency sells 20k tonnes to hold $2.40.
Infant industry: protection buys time to cut costs, if it is temporary.

notes.keyIdea: Six interventionist strategies: invest in people and infrastructure, protect and steer, and stabilise commodity prices.
takeaway: Intervention fills gaps markets leave.
Every scheme needs money, reserves or time.
Temporary and targeted beats permanent and general.

notes.title: Other Strategies and International Institutions

items.text: Lewis dual-sector model — surplus labour moves from traditional farming to a modern sector until the turning point.
Aid — resources on better-than-market terms. Debt relief — cancelling or reducing overseas debt.
World Bank — long-term development finance. IMF — short-term crisis lending with conditions. NGOs — independent non-profits.
Lewis: a wage of $3 against $2 on the farm; jobs grow 2 → 3 → 4 million until the turning point at 5 million.
Aid of 2%: growth 3% → 3.5%. Debt relief 15% → 5%: $1.2bn freed.
Tourism and primary industries share the commodity exporter's volatility.

notes.keyIdea: Industrialisation through the Lewis model, tourism, primary industries, aid and debt relief — and the World Bank, the IMF and NGOs.
takeaway: Lewis depends on reinvested profits and jobs for migrants.
Aid and relief work where the money reaches services.
The institutions differ in time scale, conditions and reach.

practice.guidance:
Two marks means two separate points. Decide what kind of measure the HDI is, and then what goes into it — listing the parts without saying they are combined into one index is only half an answer.
The HDI is a composite index of human development, published by the United Nations (1 mark), that combines three dimensions: health, measured by life expectancy at birth; education, measured by mean and expected years of schooling; and income, measured by GNI per head at purchasing power parity (1 mark). "Health, education and wealth" does not earn the second mark: the third dimension is income.
practice.question: Define the term 'Human Development Index'. (2 marks)

practice.guidance:
Calculate asks for the working as well as the answer (Appendix 6). Before any arithmetic, decide where the country sits between the two goalposts — the index is the distance above the minimum as a share of the whole range.
Health index = (actual − minimum) ÷ (maximum − minimum) = (66 − 20) ÷ (85 − 20) = 46 ÷ 65 (1 mark) = 0.708 (1 mark). Dividing 66 by 85 ignores the minimum goalpost.
practice.question: A country's life expectancy at birth is 66 years. Calculate its HDI health index, using the goalposts of 20 and 85 years. (2 marks)

practice.guidance:
Appendix 6 wants linked stages for an Explain. Start from what happens to the prices of primary products relative to manufactures over time, and carry the chain through to what the country can afford to import.
Knowledge: the Prebisch-Singer hypothesis states that the prices of primary products tend to fall over time relative to the prices of manufactured goods (1 mark). Reason: demand for primary products is income inelastic, so as world incomes rise spending on them grows more slowly (1 mark). Analysis: the terms of trade of a primary exporter therefore decline, so each unit of exports buys fewer imports (1 mark). Analysis: machinery and other capital goods cost more exports, so investment and growth are constrained (1 mark).
practice.question: Explain how dependence on primary products can constrain a developing economy's growth, with reference to the Prebisch-Singer hypothesis. (4 marks)

practice.guidance:
Calculate asks for workings (Appendix 6). Write down the model's equation before substituting anything, and read the question again for the second figure it asks for: growth of GDP and growth per head are different answers.
Growth = savings ratio ÷ capital-output ratio = 20% ÷ 5 (1 mark) = 4% a year (1 mark). Growth of GDP per head ≈ growth of GDP − population growth = 4% − 2.5% (1 mark) = 1.5% a year (1 mark). Multiplying 20 by 5 instead of dividing is the common error.
practice.question: A country saves 20% of its GDP and has a capital-output ratio of 5. Its population grows by 2.5% a year. Calculate, using the Harrod-Domar model, its annual rate of growth of GDP and of GDP per head. (4 marks)

practice.guidance:
Appendix 6 wants depth for an Analyse: one route followed through several linked stages. Decide first which dependants the question means — a young population and an ageing one constrain through different channels.
Knowledge: the dependency ratio is the number of people under 15 and over 64 for every 100 of working age (1 mark). Application: in a young, fast-growing population a large share of income goes on feeding and schooling children (1 mark). Analysis, first stage: households have little left to save, so savings available for investment are low (1 mark). Analysis, second stage: in the Harrod-Domar model, lower saving means lower investment and slower growth (1 mark). Analysis, third stage: the government must fund school places and clinics for a rising number of children, leaving less for infrastructure (1 mark). Development: income per head grows slowly when population growth absorbs most of the rise in output (1 mark).
practice.question: Analyse how a high dependency ratio may constrain growth and development in a developing economy. (6 marks)

practice.guidance:
Appendix 6 wants a chain of reasoning and a brief assessment for an Examine, so save room for a judgement. Separate the two factors before writing: taking bribes is not the same failure as courts that cannot enforce a contract.
Level 1 states that corruption harms growth, with little explanation. Level 2 explains a chain: bribes and unreliable courts raise the cost and risk of investing, so less is invested and growth slows. Level 3 develops two chains with application — public money diverted from roads and clinics, so development suffers directly; foreign investors choosing other countries, so the savings and foreign currency gaps stay open. The brief assessment that lifts an answer to the top of the range weighs how much it matters: some economies have grown fast despite corruption, and its effect depends on whether it is predictable or arbitrary and on how much investment it touches.
practice.question: Examine the impact of corruption and poor governance on growth and development in developing economies. (8 marks)

practice.guidance:
Appendix 6 wants chains of reasoning, different viewpoints and a critical assessment. Plan the case for and the case against before writing, and decide what your judgement will depend on — the kind of goods the economy exports is the obvious place to start.
Level 1 describes liberalisation with little explanation. Level 2 explains one side: larger export markets and cheaper imported inputs raise export earnings and investment, narrowing the foreign currency gap. Level 3 develops both sides with application: for it, specialisation, competition and cheaper capital goods; against it, infant industries wiped out by established rivals, deeper dependence on primary products and declining terms of trade, lost revenue from import duties, and workers in closing industries. Level 4 reaches a supported judgement that follows from the argument: liberalisation tends to help an economy with manufacturing capacity and diversified exports more than one that exports a single commodity, and it works best phased in, with support for the industries and workers that lose out.
practice.question: Discuss the likely impact of trade liberalisation on growth and development in a developing economy. (14 marks)

practice.guidance:
Appendix 6 wants multi-stage chains of reasoning, different viewpoints and informed judgements. Plan the strongest case for each approach before writing, and decide in advance what your judgement will turn on, so that the conclusion follows from the argument rather than appearing at the end.
Level 1 lists strategies with little explanation. Level 2 explains how one or two strategies work — for example, human capital raising output per worker, or FDI adding to investment. Level 3 develops both approaches with chains and application: interventionist strategies fill gaps markets leave (infrastructure, schooling, stable commodity prices) but need money, reserves and honest administration; market-orientated strategies raise efficiency and draw in foreign savings but can deepen inequality and dependence on primary products. Level 4 reaches a supported judgement: the most defensible is conditional — interventionist strategies are strongest where markets are missing and the state is capable, market-orientated ones where markets function and governance is weak, and most successful developing economies combined the two, protecting and investing while pushing firms to export.
practice.question: Evaluate the view that interventionist strategies are more effective than market-orientated strategies in promoting growth and development in developing economies. (20 marks)

practice.guidance:
Appendix 6 wants multi-stage chains of reasoning, different viewpoints and informed judgements. Start from what the model assumes, because every strong evaluation of it tests those assumptions against the economy in the question.
Level 1 describes industrialisation with little explanation. Level 2 explains the model: surplus labour in traditional farming moves to a modern sector paying a wage just above farm incomes, and reinvested profits keep creating jobs. Level 3 develops the process and its limits: output per worker rises as labour moves, incomes and tax revenue grow, and the turning point raises wages; against that, profits may be sent abroad or spent, factories may use labour-saving machines, and migrants can arrive in cities faster than jobs, leaving unemployment and slums. Level 4 reaches a supported judgement: industrialisation promotes development where profits are reinvested, industry is labour-intensive and workers have the skills to move — conditions that depend on human capital, infrastructure and governance as much as on the model itself.
practice.question: Evaluate the extent to which industrialisation, as described by the Lewis dual-sector model, can promote development in a developing economy. (20 marks)

practice.guidance:
Appendix 6 wants multi-stage chains of reasoning, different viewpoints and informed judgements. The three institutions do different jobs, so plan what each is for before judging how well it does it.
Level 1 describes one institution with little explanation. Level 2 explains their roles: the World Bank finances long-term development projects; the IMF lends short-term to countries in balance of payments crises; NGOs deliver aid and services directly to communities. Level 3 develops their effects on both sides: World Bank projects build infrastructure and human capital but can add to debt and suit donors' priorities; IMF loans restore stability and confidence but their conditions can cut health and education spending and deepen recessions; NGOs reach the poorest at low cost but on a small scale and with uncertain funding. Level 4 reaches a supported judgement: their contributions complement one another, and their effectiveness depends on the country's governance and on whether conditions and projects fit its circumstances.
practice.question: Evaluate the role of the World Bank, the International Monetary Fund and non-government organisations in promoting growth and development. (20 marks)

quiz.question: A country's life expectancy at birth is 50 years. Using HDI goalposts of 20 and 85 years, its health index is:
quiz.explanation: The index is the distance above the minimum as a share of the whole range: (50 − 20) ÷ (85 − 20) = 30 ÷ 65 = 0.462. Dividing 50 by 85, or by 65, ignores the minimum goalpost.

quiz.question: Copper is 50% of a country's export earnings and its world price falls by 20%. Export earnings fall by:
quiz.explanation: The fall in earnings is the good's share of exports times the fall in its price: 0.5 × 20% = 10%. Using the price fall alone assumes copper is all the country exports.

quiz.question: A country has 40% of its people under 15, 5% over 64 and 55% of working age. Its dependency ratio is about:
quiz.explanation: The dependency ratio is (young + old) ÷ working age × 100 = 45 ÷ 55 × 100 = 82. Inverting the fraction gives 122.

options: lowers the tax rate on profits
raises the cost and risk of investing
quiz.question: Corruption constrains investment mainly because it:
quiz.explanation: Bribes and unreliable decisions act like a tax on investment: a firm needs a higher expected return before it invests, so less is invested.

options: reducing imports of machinery and fuel
raising export earnings as firms reach larger markets
quiz.question: Trade liberalisation is most likely to narrow a developing economy's foreign currency gap by:
quiz.explanation: Open markets let exporters sell more abroad, which earns the foreign currency that pays for imports. Raising duties and banning foreign ownership are the opposite of liberalisation.

options: it can never match imports on cost
its costs are high until it grows and learns
quiz.question: The infant industry argument for protection says a new industry needs shelter because:
quiz.explanation: A new industry is small and inexperienced, so its costs start high. Temporary protection gives it time to grow and cut them; the argument fails if it can never compete.

options: extra output is close to zero
jobs are in the modern sector
quiz.question: In the Lewis dual-sector model, surplus labour refers to farm workers whose:
quiz.explanation: There are so many workers on the land that removing some barely reduces the harvest, so they can move to the modern sector at almost no cost to farm output.

quiz.question: Which of these is one of the three components of the Human Development Index?
quiz.explanation: The HDI combines health, measured by life expectancy at birth, with education and income. Unemployment, inflation and the budget balance are measures of macroeconomic performance, not of human development.

options: covers health and education, not just output
measures only the rise in real GDP
quiz.question: Economic development differs from economic growth because development:
quiz.explanation: Growth is a rise in real output. Development is a rise in the quality of people's lives — longer lives, more schooling, higher incomes shared more widely — which growth can help pay for but does not guarantee.

quiz.question: The HDI combines its three dimension indices by taking:
quiz.explanation: The HDI is the cube root of the product of the three indices. A geometric mean means a very weak dimension pulls the index down more than it would in an ordinary average.

flashcards.back: Growth is a rise in real GDP. Development is a rise in the quality of people's lives — health, education, income shared widely — which growth can help pay for but does not guarantee.

steps: The world copper price falls 25%. Copper is 60% of Karanda's export earnings.
With less foreign currency, the foreign currency gap of $2bn widens.
Tax revenue from the mines falls, and the government postpones roads and schools.
Firms cannot import the machinery they planned to buy, so investment and growth fall.
chains.title: From a copper price fall to slower growth
chains.result: A commodity price fall hits growth through export earnings, tax revenue and foreign currency at once — which is why volatility of commodity prices is the first economic constraint the specification lists.

evaluation.title: Market-orientated or interventionist?
evaluation.content: Neither list wins in general, and an answer that declares one correct has missed the point. **Each strategy answers a constraint, and each needs conditions to work.** Market-orientated strategies raise efficiency and draw in foreign savings where markets function; interventionist strategies fill gaps where markets are missing, but need money, reserves and capable, honest administration. The strongest judgements name the constraint that binds hardest in the country in question — savings, foreign currency, skills, infrastructure or governance — and choose the strategy that relaxes it.
